summary: Describes best current practice on how devices, networks and services using IETF protocols should use existing standards to make emergency calls over IP networks.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6881 describes how Internet-connected phones and networks should handle emergency calls. It covers recognizing the call, finding and sending the caller's location, routing to the correct PSAP, and supporting callbacks.

subtitle: Requirements for devices, networks, and services that place emergency calls using Internet protocols.

tldr.problem: An Internet call may originate anywhere, but emergency services cover local areas. The call must be identified, associated with a location, and routed to the appropriate Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP).
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6881 gives requirements for endpoints, access networks, service providers, and intermediate devices to identify emergency calls, obtain and convey location, map it to a PSAP with LoST, and signal the call with SIP.
tldr.outcome: The document describes best current practice for interoperable emergency calling. RFC 6881 was updated by RFC 7840 and RFC 7852.

facts.label: Location-by-value update limit
facts.value: No more than one every 10 seconds

facts.label: Full test interval
facts.value: Approximately 30 days, at a random interval

today: RFC 6881 is Best Current Practice 181 and has been updated by RFC 7840 and RFC 7852. Read both updates alongside this document.

sections.title: Scope and Roles
sections.content:
RFC 6881 describes how access networks, Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) user agents, proxy servers, and Public Safety Answering Points (PSAPs) support emergency calling. It complements RFC 6443, which the RFC says is necessary to understand this document.

Requirements are labeled by the entity expected to meet them: ED- for end devices and applications, AN- for access networks, SP- for service providers, and INT- for intermediate devices such as a home router. Local regulations can affect whether access-network requirements apply.

The end-to-end flow identifies an emergency call with a service URN, obtains a location, and conveys it in SIP signaling. The Location-to-Service Translation (LoST) protocol maps the location to a PSAP URI or an Emergency Services Routing Proxy URI.
sections.plainLanguage: The document assigns requirements to the phone, access network, service provider, and devices between them. Together, those parts identify an emergency call, attach location information, and route it to a PSAP.

sections.title: Recognizing an Emergency Call
sections.content:
A device or application that implements SIP calling should support emergency calling, and a service provider that supports a device expecting to call for help must facilitate it. Endpoints should recognize emergency dial strings; a proxy should do so if the endpoint does not.

An emergency INVITE must be marked with a service URN in its Request-URI. Endpoints and service providers must recognize geographically local dial strings, and devices must be configurable with the home country used to determine home dial strings. Emergency dial strings should be learned from LoST, though they may be configured directly.

Endpoints that do not recognize a dial string should send it using the dial string URI format in RFC 4967. Endpoints and service providers must recognize all sub-services of the sos service tree. Devices should not offer one-button emergency call initiation.
sections.plainLanguage: The endpoint or proxy must identify the call as an emergency using a service URN. The system also needs to recognize emergency numbers that apply where the caller is located.

sections.title: Obtaining and Sending Location
sections.content:
Emergency calls can use civic location, such as an address, or geospatial location, such as coordinates. Endpoints, intermediate devices, and service providers must handle both forms and must not convert between them before the PSAP receives the location. The RFC permits any location-determination method if its accuracy meets local requirements.

Devices must support both DHCP location options and HTTP-Enabled Location Delivery (HELD); an access network must support at least one. Endpoints should try supported location protocols and use the first one that succeeds. With HELD, a request for routing location uses emergencyRouting; a separate request for emergencyDispatch is needed if dispatch location will be sent.

When the access network cannot determine the caller's location, it must provide a default marked method=Default. Location is conveyed in SIP using RFC 6442. Location determination is recommended to take no longer than 250 ms for routing, with typical response time under 100 ms. Updates sent by value should be no more frequent than one every 10 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone or network obtains a civic address or coordinates and sends that location with the SIP call. If the network cannot determine an exact location, it sends a marked default location.

sections.title: Mapping Location to a PSAP
sections.content:
Endpoints must support discovery of a Location Information Server (LIS) and a LoST server, learn their public IP address, and have a configurable default LoST server. If DHCP provides a LoST server, the endpoint must try it before configured servers.

An endpoint that obtains its own location should use LoST to map it to a PSAP URI. It should update the mapping when location crosses a service boundary or the mapping's time-to-live expires, and cache the result. At call time, the endpoint must try to refresh its location and should try to refresh its mapping. If a quick update fails, it uses cached information; if it has no cached mapping, it sends the call without a PSAP Route header.

A proxy on the outbound path must recognize emergency service URNs. If the call lacks a Route header, the proxy performs the LoST mapping and inserts one. If the proxy cannot obtain a mapping, it must provide a default mapping.
sections.plainLanguage: LoST uses the caller's location to return a PSAP address. The endpoint caches that result, and a proxy can perform the lookup if the endpoint has no route.

sections.title: SIP Signaling and Transport Security
sections.content:
The initial SIP message is an INVITE. Its Request-URI and To header should contain the appropriate emergency service URN; if the device cannot interpret local dial strings, they must contain a dial string URI with the dialed digits. A Route header should carry the PSAP URI obtained from LoST.

A globally routable Contact URI must remain valid for several minutes after the call, when the user agent remains registered, so an immediate callback can reach the device. If a device understands SIP location conveyance and has its location, it must include that location by value, by reference, or both. An SDP offer should include G.711 when voice is supported.

TLS is the primary protection for emergency-call signaling. IPsec may be used instead for any hop, but either TLS or IPsec must be attempted. If TLS setup is unavailable or fails, the call must be retried without TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: The INVITE identifies the emergency service, carries available location, and includes a callback address. The system attempts TLS or IPsec, but retries without TLS if setup fails.

sections.title: Callbacks, Media, and Test Calls
sections.content:
Callbacks to the Contact URI within 30 minutes of an emergency call must reach the device despite do-not-disturb or call-forwarding features. Devices must also provide a persistent address of record for later return calls, though those calls may not reach the original device. Features that interrupt emergency calls or callbacks must be disabled for the periods described in the RFC.

Endpoints send and receive media over RTP and use SIP offer/answer. G.711 A-law, and mu-law when intended for North America, must be supported; a transcoder must be used if needed to offer G.711 to the PSAP. Silence suppression must not be used, because background sound may help call takers determine what is happening.

An INVITE to a test service URN requests an automated test. User agents should run a full test after a qualifying IP address change and about every 30 days at a random interval. They must not place a test call immediately after booting.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone keeps a route open for callbacks and disables features that could interrupt the call. Test calls check the service separately and should be spaced over time.

sections.title: Security Trade-offs
sections.content:
The RFC recommends TLS or IPsec hop by hop to protect location and identity information. If establishing that protection fails, the call must be retried without it. The document prioritizes completing an emergency call over protecting the data and notes that a call without security may reveal user information, including location.

Other requirements address spoofing and routing. DHCP location implementations should use DHCP message authentication, although providing credentials can be difficult. S/MIME is not recommended because proxies need access to location information to route the call.
sections.plainLanguage: Security protects location and identity, but a failed security setup must not block the emergency call. Without protection, information such as location may be exposed.
